evals.name: smu-iv-sweep-app
evals.prompt: We have a Keithley 2450 source meter on the bench (USB, talks SCPI through pyvisa). I want a small desktop app in python where I set a start voltage, stop voltage and step, hit go, and it sweeps and plots current vs voltage live while it's measuring, and saves every sweep so I can compare them later. Compliance current needs to be settable too, our samples are thin films and we've blown a couple. Can you write it for me?
evals.expected_output: A runnable Tkinter app with the driver on a worker thread (not the Tk thread), a simulated SMU so it runs with no hardware, queue-based communication, live plotting, per-sweep session logging, and a compliance limit treated as a safety setting.
assertions: The instrument is driven from a background thread, not from the Tk callback chain: there is a threading.Thread (or equivalent) that owns the driver.
The worker communicates with the GUI through a queue rather than touching widgets directly.
A simulated/mock SMU class exists with the same interface as the real driver, so the app can run with no hardware attached.
The app can actually be launched and exercised without a Keithley connected (a --simulate flag, a checkbox, or an automatic fallback).
Each sweep is written to disk in its own identifiable file or folder, not appended into one anonymous blob.
The settings that define a sweep (start, stop, step, compliance) are recorded alongside the data, not only shown in the UI.
Compliance current is treated as a safety limit: it is set on the instrument before the output is enabled, and/or a compliance trip is detected and surfaced.
The instrument output is switched off on disconnect/close/error, so quitting cannot leave the sample energised.
Python files compile without syntax errors.

evals.name: anneal-phase-protocol
evals.prompt: I need to record our TC300 temperature controller while a sample anneals. The protocol is: hold at room temp for 5 min to get a baseline, ramp to 180 C, hold there for 20 min, then cool back down. For the analysis afterwards I absolutely need to know exactly when each stage started and stopped, because I'm correlating it against spectra from another instrument. Last time I wrote the times down on paper and it was a mess. Can you build me something for this?
evals.expected_output: An app with an explicit phase state machine, per-sample phase labelling and elapsed-time columns, a phase log with entry/exit timestamps, a protocol snapshot, and a run summary distinguishing completed from aborted runs.
assertions: There is an explicit phase/state machine with named phases (baseline, ramp, hold, cool) rather than ad-hoc timing logic scattered in callbacks.
Each phase transition is recorded with an absolute timestamp.
A per-phase log file or table is written with entry and exit times for every phase.
Every recorded sample carries which phase it belongs to.
Every recorded sample carries an elapsed-time column relative to run start and/or phase start, so analysis does not have to re-derive it from timestamps.
The protocol settings are snapshotted to a file at run start, so the run is reproducible.
A run summary distinguishes a completed run from an aborted/interrupted one.
The temperature controller is read on a background thread, not on the Tk callback chain.
A simulated temperature controller exists so the app runs with no hardware.
Python files compile without syntax errors.

evals.name: debug-freezing-monitor
evals.prompt: This is the photodiode logger we use day to day. It's fine at 200 ms per reading but if I set the interval down to 20 ms the window goes completely unresponsive - the plot stops updating and I have to kill it from task manager. The saved files are also really slow to write and I don't know why. Can you work out what's going on and fix it?
evals.expected_output: Diagnosis of the blocking driver call on the Tk thread and of savez_compressed's cost, plus a corrected version using a worker thread, a queue, a throttled redraw that reuses artists, and uncompressed saves.
assertions: Identifies the root cause of the freeze: the blocking DAQ read runs on the Tk thread inside the after() callback chain, so the event loop cannot service the UI.
Explains why shortening the interval makes it worse rather than better (the per-cycle work exceeds the scheduling interval, so the loop never catches up).
Identifies np.savez_compressed as the cause of the slow writes, and that compression buys little on noisy float data.
The fix moves the blocking read onto a worker thread.
The fix uses a queue to hand data from the worker to the GUI.
The fix replaces savez_compressed with an uncompressed save (or otherwise removes the per-sample compression cost).
The fix stops calling ax.clear() + full replot every frame, reusing the line artist with set_data instead.
The redraw rate is throttled independently of the acquisition rate, rather than redrawing once per sample.
The explanation is specific to this file (names the actual functions/lines involved) rather than generic advice.
Python files compile without syntax errors.
